shape-01.title: Before you know a sign, you know its shape
shape-01.body: Every German traffic sign belongs to one of four basic shapes - and that shape already tells you what kind of rule applies, before you've even read the symbol in detail. That's not a coincidence, it's by design: the StVO groups signs exactly along these lines.

shape-02.title: Triangle = warning sign
shape-02.body: A white or yellow triangle with a red border warns you about a hazard ahead - a curve, wildlife crossing, roadworks. It's advisory, not a strict command: you adapt your behavior to the situation, but the sign itself doesn't directly prohibit or require anything.

shape-03.title: Red circle = prohibition sign
shape-03.body: A circle with a red border is a hard prohibition - no overtaking, no entry, a speed limit. Unlike the triangle, there's no room for interpretation here: the prohibition simply applies.

shape-04.title: Blue circle = mandatory sign
shape-04.body: A blue, usually round background with a white symbol makes an action mandatory - use the bike path, a minimum speed, a required direction of travel. Like the prohibition sign, this is binding - just a 'must' instead of a 'must not'.

shape-05.title: Rectangle = guidance/information sign
shape-05.body: Rectangular signs in various colors give orientation and information - a priority road, a one-way street, a parking area, a town-entry sign. They generally don't prohibit or mandate anything directly - they explain the traffic situation to you.

shape-06.title: Why signs are only readable from one side
shape-06.body: Real traffic signs are deliberately designed so the back is unreadable or plain gray - specifically so a driver approaching from the opposite direction or a crossing street doesn't read a sign that was never meant for them. That's why drivers at the same intersection often face different rules depending on which direction they're coming from - which is the core idea behind many right-of-way situations.

vorfahrt-primer-01.title: What is "right of way" about?
vorfahrt-primer-01.body: Right of way determines who gets to go first at an intersection or junction. It's one of the most important topics on the theory exam, because right-of-way mistakes are among the most common and most dangerous causes of real-world accidents. Once you get this topic, you basically understand how traffic organizes itself at every crossing.

vorfahrt-primer-02.title: The default rule: right before left
vorfahrt-primer-02.body: If an intersection has no signs and no traffic light, the default kicks in automatically: the vehicle coming from the right has priority (§8(1) StVO). This is the baseline setting of German traffic law - the starting point that every other rule is an exception to.

vorfahrt-primer-03.title: Why right, of all directions?
vorfahrt-primer-03.body: Right-before-left works because it's a simple rule that applies everywhere - nobody has to guess or negotiate who goes first. That same idea of predictability is behind almost every right-of-way rule: signs, traffic lights, and special cases exist to add extra clarity on busier or more confusing roads, where the plain default rule alone wouldn't be enough.

vorfahrt-primer-04.title: When signs change the game
vorfahrt-primer-04.body: As soon as a sign is present, it overrides right-before-left. Sign 301 gives you priority only at that one spot, while sign 306 gives it to you along the entire road, until sign 307 cancels it. Sign 205 (yield) doesn't necessarily require a full stop if you have a clear view - but sign 206 (STOP) always does, whether or not there's any traffic in sight.

vorfahrt-primer-05.title: Three special cases that surprise people
vorfahrt-primer-05.body: In a roundabout, traffic already circulating has priority - anyone entering has to wait. A tram essentially always has right of way, no matter which direction it's coming from. And if you want to turn left, you have to let oncoming traffic going straight or turning right go first - when two cars turn left toward each other at the same time, they typically pass 'nose to nose', right side to right side.

vorfahrt-primer-06.title: The trap: "yield" doesn't always mean "stop"
vorfahrt-primer-06.body: The most common mistake is mixing up signs 205 and 206. Many people assume every 'yield' sign requires a full stop - that's only true for the octagonal STOP sign (206). With sign 205, slowing down and checking the road is enough, as long as your view is genuinely clear. Stopping out of habit isn't wrong in real life, but on the exam, the distinction is exactly what's being tested.

vorfahrt-primer-07.title: Your turn now
vorfahrt-primer-07.body: You've got the basic framework: right-before-left as the default, signs and special cases as exceptions. The rest comes with practice - so go ahead and try a few 'right of way and intersections' questions now, while it's all still fresh.

verkehrszeichen-primer-01.title: Why traffic signs are the backbone of German road law
verkehrszeichen-primer-01.body: Traffic signs are the language of the road: they tell you in a split second what's allowed, forbidden, or dangerous, without needing to read a law book. In the theory exam they show up almost everywhere – as standalone questions about a sign's meaning, but also hidden inside questions about right-of-way, parking, or speed. If you understand the underlying system, you can answer a lot of exam questions correctly even without having memorized every single sign.

verkehrszeichen-primer-02.title: The core rule: shape and color reveal the meaning
verkehrszeichen-primer-02.body: German traffic signs fall into categories you can recognize from their shape and color alone, often before you've even parsed the symbol. Round signs with a red border are usually prohibitions or restrictions (like sign 274 for maximum speed, or sign 250 banning all vehicles). Triangular signs with a red border and the point facing up warn of danger (like sign 101 for a general hazard, or sign 136 for children at play). Rectangular or square signs in blue or yellow usually give directions or instructions. This basic logic lets you correctly interpret even a sign you don't specifically remember.

verkehrszeichen-primer-03.title: The logic behind the design
verkehrszeichen-primer-03.body: This consistent shape-and-color logic exists so you can correctly read a sign instantly, even in bad visibility, at high speed, or in an unfamiliar town, without needing to stop and study it. A round red sign tells your brain from a distance 'a restriction applies here'; a red triangle says 'danger ahead'. That's exactly why the theory exam doesn't just test whether you know individual signs, but whether you've internalized the underlying system — because in real traffic, that recognition speed can be the difference between reacting in time and not.

verkehrszeichen-primer-04.title: One sign can cancel another
verkehrszeichen-primer-04.body: A key detail: many signs come in a 'positive' and a 'negative' pair. Sign 274 shows a speed limit (like '50' in black on a white background with a red border), while sign 278 – the same design but crossed out in gray – marks the end of that limit. This 'crossed-out cancellation' pattern recurs across many rules: a crossed-out sign doesn't introduce a new meaning of its own, it simply lifts whatever was ordered before.

verkehrszeichen-primer-05.title: The trap: prohibition signs often look deceptively similar
verkehrszeichen-primer-05.body: A common stumbling block in the exam: round red signs with no symbol, or with very similar symbols, get mixed up easily. Sign 267 (a white horizontal bar) bans entry for all vehicles in that direction — typically found at the end of a one-way street. Sign 250 (no symbol at all) also bans all vehicles, but for the whole stretch of road, not just one direction of entry. Sign 260 (a car and motorcycle), by contrast, only bans motor vehicles — bicycles are still allowed. When a question involves signs like these, read carefully whether it's about a direction of entry or an entire stretch of road — that distinction often decides right versus wrong.

verkehrszeichen-primer-06.title: Level crossings: recognizing the two warning stages
verkehrszeichen-primer-06.body: Another detail that's easy to confuse: the triangular warning sign with a train symbol (like sign 151) announces an unguarded level crossing from a distance — this calls for extra caution while you're still approaching. The St. Andrew's cross (sign 201), the white sign with the red X, sits right at the crossing itself and means: if a train is approaching, you must come to a full stop. So the two signs belong to different phases of the same hazard — first the advance warning from afar, then the mandatory stop right at the crossing.

verkehrszeichen-primer-07.title: Now it's your turn
verkehrszeichen-primer-07.body: You now know the core principle: shape and color set the category, symbols fill in the details, and some signs cancel others out. That's a solid foundation — the rest comes from working through real exam questions on individual signs, which naturally builds your instinct for the patterns. Go ahead and start practicing the traffic-sign questions now, and see how much you can already get right!

gefahr-primer-01.title: Hazard Perception: Why This Topic Matters
gefahr-primer-01.body: Hazard perception (Gefahrenlehre) isn't about signs or right-of-way rules — it's about what happens in between them: recognizing danger before it turns into a crash. Wet roads, black ice, a ball rolling into the street, a bus signaling to pull out, the blind spot — these are situations where simply knowing the law isn't enough. You need to anticipate and react correctly. The exam leans hard on this topic because misjudging these moments is a leading cause of serious accidents.

gefahr-primer-02.title: The Core Concept: Stopping Distance and Following Gap
gefahr-primer-02.body: The central building block of hazard perception is stopping distance: how far a vehicle travels before it comes to a stop. It's made up of reaction distance (before braking even starts) and braking distance (until the car actually stops). At 80 km/h, reaction alone eats up roughly 24 meters before your foot even hits the brake. That's why keeping enough distance from the car ahead isn't just courtesy — it's physics: your gap has to be big enough to cover your own full stopping distance.

gefahr-primer-03.title: The Logic Behind the Rules
gefahr-primer-03.body: The reasoning is straightforward: tires need friction against the road to steer and brake. Anything that reduces that friction — rain, ice, worn tread, low tire pressure — automatically lengthens braking distance. And humans need time to notice a hazard and react, no matter how alert they are. Rules of thumb like 'half your speedometer reading' or the three-second rule exist because people tend to underestimate how much time and distance that reaction really costs. Once this clicks, you'll see why the exam always ties speed and following distance together.

gefahr-primer-04.title: Special Case: Aquaplaning
gefahr-primer-04.body: One especially important special case is aquaplaning (hydroplaning): with enough standing water and high speed, a wedge of water can lift the tires completely off the asphalt. The car then loses contact with the road and becomes almost impossible to steer or brake. The correct response goes against instinct: ease off the gas, hold the steering wheel steady and straight, and avoid hard braking until the tires regain grip. A second winter-specific case: black ice forms first on bridges (they cool from both above and below) and in shaded, damp spots — even when the rest of the road still looks dry.

gefahr-primer-05.title: The Trap: Warning Signs People Miss
gefahr-primer-05.body: A classic exam mistake is reacting only to visible dangers instead of the early signals that precede them. A ball rolling into the road is harmless by itself — the real danger is the child who's about to run after it. The blind spot works the same way: people assume mirrors cover everything, but there's a zone right beside and slightly behind the car that neither the interior nor the side mirrors show. That's exactly why the exam likes to test whether you can infer the real hazard from a seemingly minor detail, not just whether you spot the obvious one.

gefahr-primer-06.title: Another Nuance: Reading Other Road Users
gefahr-primer-06.body: Hazard perception also means correctly interpreting what other road users are about to do. A bus signaling from a stop is announcing that it wants to pull back into traffic — as the driver of another vehicle, you need to adjust your speed so you can let it in if necessary. This shows that recognizing hazards isn't only about road surface and weather; it's also about anticipating other people's intentions before a critical situation develops.

gefahr-primer-07.title: Now It's Your Turn
gefahr-primer-07.body: You now have the basic framework for hazard perception: stopping distance, friction, common danger situations, and the skill of spotting early warning signs instead of just obvious dangers. The rest comes from practice — the more real exam questions you work through, the faster theory turns into reflex. So go ahead: start practicing questions on this topic now and see how much has already stuck.

umwelt-primer-01.title: What is 'Environmentally Conscious Driving' about?
umwelt-primer-01.body: This topic tests whether you know how to save fuel, cut emissions, and keep your vehicle in a safe, environmentally sound condition. It ties together two things that might seem unrelated at first: your driving style (how you accelerate, shift gears, brake) and your car's technical condition (tires, driver-assist systems, roadworthiness inspections). Both show up regularly in the theory exam, and both have a real-world effect on fuel consumption, safety, and emissions.

umwelt-primer-02.title: The core rule: look ahead, shift up early
umwelt-primer-02.body: The key takeaway for this area is: anticipatory driving saves the most fuel. In practice that means scanning traffic well ahead, avoiding unnecessary braking and accelerating, and shifting into a higher gear early. That keeps engine revs low and the engine running efficiently. This single idea - 'look ahead, shift up early' - is the answer you should reach for first in many exam questions on this topic.

umwelt-primer-03.title: The logic behind it
umwelt-primer-03.body: A car that constantly brakes hard and then accelerates again burns noticeably more fuel than one that flows smoothly with traffic - every hard brake destroys kinetic energy that fuel was just spent creating. That's exactly why driving style and environmental awareness are so closely linked: less braking and gassing means less wasted energy, lower consumption, and lower emissions. For the same reason, vehicle maintenance matters too - a poorly maintained car (say, with underinflated tires) burns more fuel even if your driving style is perfect.

umwelt-primer-04.title: A detail often overlooked: tire pressure and shutting off the engine in traffic
umwelt-primer-04.body: Underinflated tires increase rolling resistance - fuel consumption rises, and braking distance can even get longer at the same time. That's why checking tire pressure regularly pays off twice: for your wallet and for safety. Here's a second practical example from the exam: if traffic is stopped and expected to stay stopped for more than a minute (say, in a jam), you should switch off the engine. Many modern cars do this automatically via start-stop systems, but you should know the underlying principle.

umwelt-primer-05.title: The trap: this topic is not just about saving fuel
umwelt-primer-05.body: Many learners assume this topic is only about driving style and fuel economy - and get caught off guard by questions on vehicle technology and safety systems that also belong here: minimum tire tread depth (1.6 mm), the Alpine symbol for genuine winter tires, ABS, ESP, or the roadworthiness inspection (HU). The common thread isn't 'saves fuel' but 'responsible, safe, and environmentally sound vehicle use.' So don't be surprised if a question in this area suddenly asks about ABS or the HU instead of driving habits.

umwelt-primer-06.title: One more nuance: ABS and ESP are not the same thing
umwelt-primer-06.body: A common point of confusion: ABS prevents the wheels from locking up under hard braking so you stay able to steer - but it doesn't necessarily shorten your braking distance. ESP steps in earlier: it selectively brakes individual wheels to prevent the car from skidding, before things get to a full emergency stop. Remember it this way: ABS helps you while braking, ESP helps you stay on track in the first place.

umwelt-primer-07.title: Your turn now
umwelt-primer-07.body: You now know the two sides of 'Environmentally Conscious Driving': anticipatory, fuel-saving driving style on one hand, and your vehicle's technical condition and safety systems on the other. They belong together because both reflect how responsibly you handle your car. The best way to lock this in is with real practice questions - go try a few from this topic now and see how confident you're already feeling!

verhalten-primer-01.title: What does 'Conduct in Road Traffic' cover?
verhalten-primer-01.body: This topic bundles the everyday duties that don't fall under right-of-way or road signs, but show up just as often on the exam: how to react to police hand signals, what to do first at an accident, the rules for towing a broken-down car, and who in the vehicle must wear a seatbelt. It's a catch-all for obligations that matter constantly in real driving - and the exam expects you not just to recognize them, but to apply them in the right order.

verhalten-primer-02.title: The core idea: safety before convenience
verhalten-primer-02.body: The thread running through this topic is simple: in almost every situation there's a clear rule that puts safety ahead of convenience. Seatbelt obligation applies to every seat, including the back seat. You can't pick up your phone while the engine is running, even if you're just sitting at a red light. Children under 12 or shorter than 150 cm need a proper child seat. These rules feel strict on purpose - they take the 'just this once' judgment call out of your hands.

verhalten-primer-03.title: Why so strict? Because seconds decide outcomes
verhalten-primer-03.body: These rules can look overcautious at first glance, but they come straight from real accident patterns. A phone in your hand distracts you even while stationary and slows your reaction when the light changes or a pedestrian steps out. An unbuckled passenger becomes a projectile in a crash and endangers everyone else in the car. And if you're first on the scene of an accident, you often have only minutes where doing things in the right order makes the difference - which is why the sequence (secure the scene, then help, then call emergency services) is fixed, not just a suggestion.

verhalten-primer-04.title: A detail people often miss: police hand signals
verhalten-primer-04.body: A police officer raising one arm straight up is a general stop signal - all traffic from every direction must halt. If the officer instead stretches an arm out to the side, it acts like a red light only for traffic crossing the imagined line of that arm; traffic moving parallel to the arm may continue. The exam likes to exploit the difference between these two signals as a mix-up trap, so it's worth keeping the two images clearly separate in your mind.

verhalten-primer-05.title: The trap: 'engine running' is not the same as 'car moving'
verhalten-primer-05.body: Many learners assume the phone ban only applies while actually driving. In reality, what matters is whether the engine is running - if you're stopped at a red light with the engine on, you still can't pick up your phone. Only with the engine switched off is phone use allowed. This distinction between 'driving' and 'engine running' comes up again and again on the exam, and it's a classic spot where otherwise well-prepared candidates trip up.

verhalten-primer-06.title: Another special case: towing has its own rules
verhalten-primer-06.body: When a broken-down vehicle is towed, a separate speed limit of 40 km/h applies, unless an even lower limit is in force. Whoever sits at the wheel of the towed vehicle needs a valid driving license and must be able to steer and brake at any moment - simply being pulled along passively isn't enough. Details like this show that 'Conduct in Traffic' is often built from many small but very concretely testable numbers and conditions.

verhalten-primer-07.title: Now it's your turn
verhalten-primer-07.body: You now know the key building blocks: police hand signals, seatbelt and child-seat rules, what to do at an accident scene, and the special rules for towing. The best way to really lock this in is to work through real exam questions on this topic now - you'll run into these exact traps again, but phrased the way the actual exam asks them. So go ahead: start practicing questions on 'Conduct in Road Traffic' and put what you just read to use.

autobahn-primer-01.title: What "Motorways and Expressways" covers
autobahn-primer-01.body: The Autobahn is the road category with the highest speeds allowed – and that's exactly why it comes with its own strict set of rules. This topic isn't about new road signs; it's a self-contained rulebook: who's even allowed on, how to overtake safely, what to do in a traffic jam, and what happens if you miss your exit. These questions show up again and again in the exam, and a few of them – like forming an emergency corridor – are flagged as "high-stakes" because getting them wrong in real life can cost lives.

autobahn-primer-02.title: The core rule: not everyone – and not everything – belongs on the motorway
autobahn-primer-02.body: The Autobahn has a minimum speed requirement – if your vehicle can't reach it, you're not allowed on in the first place. That's why pedestrians, bicycles, and mopeds (Mofas) are banned outright, along with any vehicle that technically can't exceed a certain speed threshold. This one idea – "only those who can keep up get to join" – is the thread connecting many exam questions on this topic.

autobahn-primer-03.title: Why these rules exist
autobahn-primer-03.body: Motorways only work if traffic keeps flowing smoothly and quickly. A single very slow vehicle – whether a moped or a car crawling at 40 km/h for no good reason – forces everyone else into sudden braking and risky maneuvers. That's exactly why driving unusually slowly without a valid reason is banned, even though there's no general speed limit: safety on the Autobahn comes from predictability, not just from speed itself.

autobahn-primer-04.title: A fact many people underestimate: the emergency corridor
autobahn-primer-04.body: As soon as traffic slows to a crawl or comes to a stop, you must form an emergency corridor (Rettungsgasse) immediately – not just once you actually see an ambulance or fire truck approaching. This is one of the most important points in the whole motorway chapter, because every second counts when emergency responders need to reach a crash.

autobahn-primer-05.title: The trap: "I missed my exit, now what?"
autobahn-primer-05.body: A classic mistake in the exam – and in real driving: if you miss your exit, you must never turn around or reverse to try to reach it. Both are strictly forbidden on the Autobahn and extremely dangerous, since traffic behind you is moving at high speed. The only correct answer is always: keep driving to the next exit.

autobahn-primer-06.title: Overtaking has clear rules of its own
autobahn-primer-06.body: On the Autobahn, overtaking is normally only allowed on the left – passing on the right is only permitted when traffic on all lanes is congested and moving slowly. After overtaking, you may only merge back to the right once you can clearly see the overtaken vehicle in your rearview mirror. And wherever a solid line separates lanes, crossing it to overtake is off-limits, no matter how much room it looks like there is.

autobahn-primer-07.title: Now you're ready for the real questions
autobahn-primer-07.body: You now know the key building blocks: who's allowed on the motorway, why speed and behavior are regulated so strictly, and the spots where most people trip up – emergency corridors, missed exits, overtaking rules. That's a solid enough foundation to jump straight into the practice questions on this topic. Good luck – and remember, the high-stakes questions especially are worth practicing thoroughly!

parken-primer-01.title: Why parking and stopping rules get their own exam topic
parken-primer-01.body: Parking and stopping sounds trivial, but it's one of the areas where everyday mistakes happen most often — and where the exam loves sneaky detail questions. This topic covers the rules for where, how long, and under what conditions you're allowed to leave your vehicle at the roadside. It sounds simple, but there are plenty of exceptions and distance requirements you should have down cold before you start practicing questions.

parken-primer-02.title: The core distinction: stopping vs. parking
parken-primer-02.body: Everything in this topic rests on one distinction, defined in §12(2) StVO: stopping is a brief pause in your journey, for example to let someone in or out. Parking begins as soon as you stop for more than three minutes or leave the vehicle. This matters because many restrictions only apply to parking — if you're just stopping briefly, some things are allowed that would be forbidden if you parked.

parken-primer-03.title: The logic behind the rules
parken-primer-03.body: Almost all parking rules boil down to one principle: parked vehicles must not block visibility or space. A parked car is immobile — if it's in the wrong spot, it permanently obstructs the view at intersections, blocks driveways, or leaves no room for traffic to pass. That's why the rules are anchored to specific danger points like intersections, driveway entrances, and pedestrian crossings — exactly where clear sightlines and free passage matter most.

parken-primer-04.title: The 5-meter rule: your most important number
parken-primer-04.body: One figure comes up again and again in this topic: 5 meters. You may not park within 5 meters before or after an intersection (§12(3) StVO), and not within 5 meters before a pedestrian crossing (§12(3) StVO). The reasoning is the same as before: at that distance, drivers, other road users, and pedestrians need to be able to see each other in time. Memorize this number well — it shows up on the exam more often than you'd expect.

parken-primer-05.title: The trap: 'never park without lights at night' is wrong
parken-primer-05.body: Many learner drivers assume parked cars always need lights on at night. In fact, on sufficiently lit streets with a speed limit of up to 50 km/h, you're allowed to park with no extra lighting at all (§17(4) StVO). The exam likes to use this exception as a trick question, so read such questions carefully and watch for phrases like 'sufficiently lit' and the speed limit condition.

parken-primer-06.title: More pitfalls: second row, left side, parking discs
parken-primer-06.body: Three more points worth knowing: parking in the second row — next to already-parked cars so they get boxed in — is forbidden (§12(4) StVO). Parking on the left in the direction of travel is generally only allowed on one-way streets (§12(4) StVO). And in a zone requiring a parking disc, you must set the actual arrival time and display the disc clearly behind the windshield (§13 StVO) — not your departure time or an estimate.

parken-primer-07.title: Ready for the practice questions
parken-primer-07.body: You now know the essentials: the difference between stopping and parking, the 5-meter distance rules, the lighting exception, and typical violations like double-parking or parking on the wrong side. That's enough to dive in. Grab the real exam questions on 'parking and stopping' and put your knowledge to work right away — that's the best way to make it stick.

ladung-primer-01.title: Why load securing and transport gets its own exam topic
ladung-primer-01.body: 'Load and transport' isn't just about packing your trunk efficiently. The exam checks whether you know how to secure luggage, roof boxes, trailers, and even children so nobody gets hurt. It sounds minor, but it's genuinely safety-critical: a poorly secured load can be just as dangerous in an emergency stop as a driving mistake. This topic blends classic traffic-law knowledge (the duty to secure a load, lighting rules) with everyday situations almost every driver eventually faces — a vacation with a roof box, a bike rack, or towing a trailer.

ladung-primer-02.title: The core rule: your load must be secured so nothing can happen
ladung-primer-02.body: The heart of this topic is §22(1) StVO: any load must be stowed and secured so it can't slide, tip over, or fall off — even during an emergency stop, a sudden swerve, or on a bumpy road. That applies to your trunk just as much as to roof racks, trailers, or loose items on the back seat. It also means you can't exceed the permitted axle load or total weight — a car doesn't just need to stay under its overall weight limit, it also can't be unevenly loaded on one side.

ladung-primer-03.title: Why the rules are so strict
ladung-primer-03.body: The logic here is simple but important: an unsecured, heavy load behaves like a projectile during an emergency stop. A crate of drinks from the trunk can fly forward with serious force and badly injure passengers. At the same time, a shifting load unpredictably changes the car's center of gravity and handling — braking distance increases and steering responds differently. That's why load securing isn't a comfort issue; it's a direct road-safety question for everyone in the car and everyone else on the road.

ladung-primer-04.title: A concrete example: the best securing method is a combination
ladung-primer-04.body: One detail the exam likes to test: what secures luggage in the trunk most effectively? The answer isn't 'either/or' — it's the combination. An anti-slip mat increases friction between the load and the trunk floor (friction-based securing), while lashing straps mechanically prevent shifting on top of that (form-fit securing). Only together do they provide truly reliable protection. This same principle — friction plus mechanical fixing — comes up again in practice with roof boxes and trailer loads.

ladung-primer-05.title: The trap: lighting and visibility get overlooked
ladung-primer-05.body: A classic mistake: many people focus only on whether the load is firmly attached and forget it also mustn't obstruct anything. A rear bike rack that covers the license plate or taillights requires an additional, compliant lighting panel with its own plate and rear lights. Likewise, if a trailer is wider than the towing vehicle, extended wide-angle mirrors must be fitted if needed so the full width stays visible. Remember: load securing isn't just 'is it held tight' — it's also 'can others still see me, and can I still see enough.'

ladung-primer-06.title: Another number worth remembering: 80 km/h with a trailer
ladung-primer-06.body: Another point often tested alongside load securing: when towing a trailer on the Autobahn or expressways, a general speed limit of 80 km/h applies — regardless of the otherwise unrestricted speeds for cars without a trailer. Only with a special certification (the well-known 100-km/h sticker, which requires additional technical conditions to be met) can you go faster. This rule is a reminder that towing a trailer changes the driving rules themselves, not just the securing requirements.

ladung-primer-07.title: Now it's your turn
ladung-primer-07.body: You now know the key building blocks: the securing duty under §22 StVO, the friction-plus-straps combination, the often-forgotten lighting requirement, and the special trailer rules. That's a solid foundation to dive into real exam questions. The best way to lock it in is to try a few practice questions on 'load and transport' right now — you'll quickly see which details have stuck and where you still need to sharpen up. Go for it!

erstehilfe-primer-01.title: Why first aid and accident-scene behavior are on the exam
erstehilfe-primer-01.body: Every new driver will sooner or later pass an accident scene, or even have to act as a first responder. This topic doesn't test whether you can become a doctor or paramedic - it tests whether you can bridge those first critical minutes correctly: securing the scene, organizing help, and setting the rescue chain in motion. Those first few actions often decide whether an accident stays contained or turns into a tragedy with even more people hurt.

erstehilfe-primer-02.title: The core rule: secure, then help, then call
erstehilfe-primer-02.body: There's one consistent sequence behind every accident scene: first secure the area (turn on hazard lights, put on a hi-vis vest, set up the warning triangle), then attend to the injured, and call the emergency number 112 alongside or right after that. This order, or the logic behind it, underlies almost every exam question on this topic, even when a question only picks out a single step.

erstehilfe-primer-03.title: Why secure first instead of helping immediately?
erstehilfe-primer-03.body: This might sound harsh, but the logic holds up: if you rush straight to an injured person without securing the scene first, following vehicles can crash into the accident site and injure even more people, possibly you as the helper. That's why securing the scene comes first: only once you and oncoming traffic are no longer at additional risk can real help actually do good instead of creating new victims.

erstehilfe-primer-04.title: The warning triangle distance isn't a fixed number
erstehilfe-primer-04.body: As a rule of thumb: on rural roads you place the warning triangle about 100 meters before the accident site. But before a blind curve or the crest of a hill, drivers behind you need more reaction time, so the distance is increased noticeably, on highways figures of roughly 150 to 400 meters are common. The exam likes to test exactly this adjustment for visibility, not just the plain number 100.

erstehilfe-primer-05.title: The trap: putting on the vest only after getting out
erstehilfe-primer-05.body: A classic exam mistake is assuming you should step out first and then calmly put on the hi-vis vest. In the dark on a rural road, that's dangerous, because exactly at the moment you need to be visible outside the car, you aren't yet. The correct answer is to put the vest on while still inside the vehicle, before you get out, so you're immediately recognizable to others.

erstehilfe-primer-06.title: Checking for unconsciousness and positioning correctly
erstehilfe-primer-06.body: With an unresponsive person, first check consciousness: speak loudly and gently shake their shoulders. If there's no reaction, tilt the head back to open the airway and check for about 10 seconds by looking, listening, and feeling whether the chest rises and air is moving. If the person is breathing normally but stays unconscious, put them in the recovery position so the airway stays clear, protected from vomit or their own tongue, for instance. And whatever order you act in: the 112 emergency number works across Europe even without credit or your own provider's network coverage.

erstehilfe-primer-07.title: Now it's your turn
erstehilfe-primer-07.body: You now know the sequence, the reasoning behind it, and the typical pitfalls in first aid and accident-scene behavior. The best next step is to put this into practice with real exam questions, that's where you'll really find out if the order and the details have stuck. Time to dive into the practice questions!

fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-01.title: What this topic covers
fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-01.body: "Fitness to drive" covers everything that can impair your ability to safely operate a vehicle: alcohol, drugs, medication, and fatigue. This isn't a side topic for the exam - impairment from alcohol or exhaustion is one of the most common causes of severe accidents. The exam expects you to know specific blood-alcohol thresholds, the rules around substances, and the hidden risks of medications that seem harmless.

fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-02.title: The core rule: staggered alcohol limits
fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-02.body: Germany doesn't have one single alcohol limit - it's a tiered system. From 0.5 per mille, experienced drivers commit a regulatory offense (§24a StVG): a fine, points, usually a driving ban. From 1.1 per mille, it becomes a criminal offense - so-called "absolute unfitness to drive" under §316 StGB - regardless of whether your driving actually looked impaired. New drivers on probation and anyone under 21, however, face a strict zero-tolerance rule: 0.0 per mille (§24c StVG).

fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-03.title: Why the limits are set this way
fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-03.body: The logic: alcohol impairs reaction time, judgment, and risk assessment long before you feel drunk. That's why the criminal threshold at 1.1 per mille applies automatically - lawmakers assume that beyond this level, nobody can drive safely, no matter how experienced. The stricter zero-tolerance rule for new drivers exists because they haven't yet built the driving experience to compensate for even minor impairment - so inexperience plus alcohol multiplies the risk rather than just adding to it.

fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-04.title: The hidden threshold: 0.3 per mille
fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-04.body: Beyond the fixed limits, there's also "relative unfitness to drive": from around 0.3 per mille, a criminal offense under §316 StGB can already apply - but only if it's combined with alcohol-related driving mistakes or an accident. In other words, being under the 0.5 per mille mark doesn't automatically make you "safe" - a driving error plus alcohol in your blood can already trigger criminal liability.

fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-05.title: The trap: home remedies don't sober you up
fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-05.body: A classic exam mistake is believing that strong coffee, a cold shower, or fresh air lowers your blood alcohol level. It doesn't: only time breaks down alcohol, slowly over several hours, at a rate that varies from person to person. Coffee might make you feel more alert, but it does nothing to your actual blood alcohol content. Remember this: the belief that you can "caffeinate your way sober" is a dangerous misconception - and the exam specifically tests for it.

fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-06.title: Not just alcohol: drugs and medication
fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-06.body: For illegal drugs like cannabis or cocaine, a zero-tolerance rule generally applies (§24a StVG): a detectable trace in your blood alone can be enough for a fine or a criminal charge, regardless of the amount. But legal substances matter too: over-the-counter medications like antihistamines for allergies can cause drowsiness, and even prescribed sedatives can significantly impair your reaction time. The package leaflet often warns about this explicitly - and it's the driver's own responsibility to check their fitness to drive, whether the medication needs a prescription or not.

fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-07.title: Now it's your turn
fahrtuechtigkeit-primer-07.body: You now have the framework: the alcohol tiers at 0.0 / 0.3 / 0.5 / 1.1 per mille, the zero-tolerance rule for drugs, and the often-underestimated risks from medication and fatigue. The exact numbers and exceptions stick best through repetition. Go ahead and start the real practice questions on this topic now - that's how you turn this from theory into something you can rely on when it counts on exam day.

anhaenger_be-primer-01.title: Trailers and Class BE – what this topic covers
anhaenger_be-primer-01.body: This topic area covers everything related to towing a trailer: which license class you need, what technical checks are mandatory before you drive off, and how a car-trailer combination behaves differently from a car on its own. This isn't a niche subject — anyone who regularly tows a caravan, horse trailer, or boat trailer for work or leisure needs Class BE. And because a trailer can turn into a real hazard if something goes wrong (swaying, brake failure, jackknifing), a lot of the questions here are flagged as high-stakes for the exam.

anhaenger_be-primer-02.title: The core rule: when B is enough, and when you need BE
anhaenger_be-primer-02.body: Class B alone always covers trailers up to 750 kg permissible gross mass, regardless of how heavy your tow vehicle is. On top of that, B also lets you tow heavier trailers as long as the combined permissible mass of car plus trailer stays at or below 3,500 kg. You only need Class BE once both conditions are met at the same time: the trailer weighs more than 750 kg AND the total combination exceeds 3,500 kg. A worked example from the practice questions: a car rated at 2,000 kg towing a trailer rated at 1,800 kg gives a combination of 3,800 kg. Since the trailer is over 750 kg and the combination is over 3,500 kg, BE is required here.

anhaenger_be-primer-03.title: Why these limits? The logic behind the rule
anhaenger_be-primer-03.body: The 750 kg and 3,500 kg thresholds aren't arbitrary — they reflect how much a trailer can actually change the way the combination drives. A light trailer under 750 kg barely affects braking distance or steering behavior, so the standard Class B training is sufficient. But once the combination gets heavier and the trailer itself carries real weight, issues like braking performance, swaying, and reversing become genuine risks that require extra knowledge and practice. Class BE exists specifically to make sure you've been tested on exactly those added dangers — coupling security, noseweight, and the physics of maneuvering a trailer — before you're allowed to tow at that scale.

anhaenger_be-primer-04.title: The breakaway cable – a quiet lifesaver
anhaenger_be-primer-04.body: One detail that's easy to underestimate: the breakaway cable on braked trailers. If the trailer accidentally detaches from the tow vehicle — say, because the coupling fails — this cable automatically applies the trailer's brakes. That brings the trailer to a controlled stop instead of letting it roll away uncontrolled. It's a core safety feature you should keep in mind every time you tow a braked trailer, even though in everyday driving you'll hopefully never need it to actually trigger.

anhaenger_be-primer-05.title: The trap: steering while reversing with a trailer
anhaenger_be-primer-05.body: This is one of the classic stumbling blocks in the BE exam: when reversing, the trailer moves the opposite way from what feels intuitive. If you want the trailer's rear end to swing right, you need to turn the steering wheel left — not right, as you'd instinctively do without a trailer attached. Many test-takers fall into this trap because they steer on autopilot, the way they would without a trailer. Make a deliberate point of memorizing this reversal, because it's exactly the kind of counterintuitive detail that shows up in exam questions.

anhaenger_be-primer-06.title: Noseweight: the underrated detail before you set off
anhaenger_be-primer-06.body: Noseweight is the vertical force with which the trailer's drawbar presses down on the tow vehicle's coupling — and it has to stay within the limits set by the manufacturer. If noseweight is significantly too low, for example because heavy cargo was loaded too far back in the trailer, the drawbar becomes unstable and the trailer is more prone to swaying. Too much noseweight, on the other hand, overloads the rear axle and coupling. Both are dangerous, which is why correct loading — and therefore proper noseweight — is something you should check before any longer trip.

anhaenger_be-primer-07.title: Time to practice
anhaenger_be-primer-07.body: You now know the key building blocks: when Class B is enough and when you need BE, why the coupling, breakaway cable, and noseweight aren't just formalities but real safety factors, and why reversing with a trailer briefly rewires how your brain thinks about steering. That's a solid foundation — the rest comes with practice. Go ahead and start working through the real exam questions on this topic now, and put what you just learned to use.
